seo.title: Karmic tail 3 19 7 compatibility: a warm home, the sun and a sleigh
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 19 7 compatibility: The Empress, The Sun, The Chariot. Why a couple with a warm home must learn the road and the reins, read through Pushkin.

title: Karmic tail 3-19-7 in compatibility: “Frost and sun” and a sleigh at the door
short: The Empress, The Sun, The Chariot. The couple's karmic tail 3-19-7 looks like a greetings card: a warm home, a bright day, a sleigh waiting at the door. The puzzle is why such a couple needs a task at all. The answer lies in the order of the cards. The couple enters its task through the wish for a shared home (3), lives it out in full light, in plain view of everyone (19), and the main thing it has to learn is The Chariot (7): deciding where the two of them are going and who holds the reins.

sections.h2: Thirty lines that everyone knows by heart
paragraphs: “Winter Morning” is dated 3 November 1829. Pushkin wrote it at Pavlovskoye, the Wulf family estate in Tver province, where he was staying with friends. Whom it addresses is unknown: scholars have proposed several names, and none is proven. For our reading that is a gift — either partner can stand in the place of the “lovely friend”, and the roles here are not split by sex.

The first stanza is the sun and a sleeper: “Frost and sun — a wondrous day! / You are still dozing, lovely friend — / It's time, my beauty, wake up.” One is already at the window, the other still lost in languor. The second stanza is last night: “Last night, remember, the blizzard raged, / Haze swept across the murky sky; / The moon, like a pale blot, / Showed yellow through the gloomy clouds, / And you sat there sad — / But now… look out of the window.” The third is snow in the sun, a black see-through wood and “the stream glitters under the ice”. (Translations of Pushkin here are ours.)

The fourth stanza is the couple's tail, in order: “The whole room is lit / With an amber gleam. With a merry crackle / The stoked stove crackles. / It is pleasant to think by the stove-bench. / But you know — shouldn't we have the little brown mare / Harnessed to the sleigh?” The room is The Empress. The amber gleam that has come into it is The Sun. The sleigh is The Chariot. **Six lines, three cards in the order 3-19-7, and between comfort and the road stands a single word: “But”.**

The fifth stanza is the road itself: “Gliding over the morning snow, / Dear friend, let us give ourselves up to the run / Of the impatient horse / And visit the empty fields, / The woods, so thick not long ago, / And the shore that is dear to me.”

When the poem is reread for its pronouns, its hidden plot shows through. Until the last stanza there is only “you”: you are dozing, you remember, you sat there sad, look, you know. “We” arrives in the last stanza, and even then not as a word, only inside two Russian verbs: “let us give ourselves up”, “let us visit”. And “I” appears in the whole poem exactly once — as its last word: “the shore that is dear to me”. **The sleigh is for two, but the shore belongs to one.**

One more detail. Nobody in the poem takes the reins. Someone is told to harness the mare — other hands do the work — and then the two “give themselves up to the run of the impatient horse”. So the horse is driving. This is the main task of the 3-19-7 tail, written down almost two hundred years before any calculator: the two already sit in one sleigh, but only one has named the route, and the speed is set by whatever pulls the cart.

sections.h2: How the three numbers add up: last night's blizzard and moon
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Take a couple born on 06.03.1978 and 11.02.1976.

The first partner: day 6, month 3, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 8 = 25 → 7. Karmic task 6 + 3 + 7 = 16, centre 6 + 3 + 7 + 16 = 32 → 5. Entry of the tail 16 + 5 = 21, middle 21 + 16 = 37 → 10, task 16 — personal tail 21-10-16.
The second: day 11, month 2, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Task 11 + 2 + 5 = 18, centre 11 + 2 + 5 + 18 = 36 → 9. Entry 18 + 9 = 27 → 9, middle 9 + 18 = 27 → 9 — personal tail 9-9-18.
The couple's tail adds up point by point:
The centre of the couple's chart is 5 + 9 = 14, Temperance. The couple's values for these two are 15, The Devil.

Now the main clue. The couple's Chariot is made of two personal tasks: one partner's Tower and the other's Moon. The Tower is what collapses without warning, the storm. The Moon is night, unease, pale light through cloud. The second stanza of “Winter Morning” is exactly that sum: “the blizzard raged”, “the moon, like a pale blot, showed yellow through the gloomy clouds”. **One partner's storm and the other's moon from last night turn into a sleigh by morning.** Matching the verse to the arithmetic is our reading, but the numbers in it are real: 16 + 18 = 34 → 7.

This is how 3-19-7 forms beyond this one example too. Running through all dates gives only two combinations of personal tails, and in both one of the two was born with the tail 9-9-18: 21-10-16 + 9-9-18 in 82% of such couples and 21-10-7 + 9-9-18 in 18%. That partner has The Hermit in the centre of the personal chart and twice more in the tail, with The Moon as the task. The other partner's tail always opens with The World and The Wheel of Fortune. The 3-19-7 tail is never built from two similar personal tails: The Hermit and The World always meet in it — solitude and the wide world.

That gives the couple's three numbers. Entry: one partner's World plus the other's Hermit, 21 + 9 = 30 → 3. The huge snowy world outside and the room where “it is pleasant to think by the stove-bench” together make The Empress — a home. Middle: one partner's Wheel of Fortune plus the other's Hermit, 10 + 9 = 19 — The Sun. Task: one partner's Tower plus the other's Moon, and in 18% of couples one partner's own Chariot (tail 21-10-7) plus the same Moon: 7 + 18 = 25 → 7. Then one of the two already has a road, and someone else's night is added to it. That is the plot of another Pushkin poem; more on it below.

The couple's middle is not the reduced sum of its ends. In a personal chart the middle of the tail is the entry plus the task, and 3 + 7 would give 10, The Wheel of Fortune. That is why there is no personal tail 3-19-7. Yet The Wheel is still there in the couple's middle — not as the result but as a term of the sum: 19 = 10 + 9. One partner's Wheel, with the other's Hermit light added, becomes The Sun. Even the digits 1 and 9 add back up to 10.

The centre of the couple's chart gives away the same make-up. Temperance (14) stands there in 82.2% of such couples, The Hierophant (5) in 17.8%. The partner with the 9-9-18 tail always has The Hermit in the personal centre; the other has The Hierophant (with 21-10-16) or Temperance (with 21-10-7): 9 + 5 = 14, 9 + 14 = 23 → 5. The two cards swap places: whoever has The Hierophant in the personal centre, the couple gets Temperance in its centre, and the other way round.
The tail is rare: roughly one couple in 1,366 (0.073%), 85th place among the 97 couple tails. There are no other couple tails made of the same three numbers.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a room lit with amber (3 — The Empress)
paragraphs: The entry point is what the couple wants together, its common language. For 3-19-7 that language is home. Such a pair builds a nest first: a renovation they do together, a kitchen where everyone gathers, plants on the windowsill, Sunday bread from their own oven. Guests leave them warmed through. Among Lisovskaya's meanings of The Empress in a couple there is also this one: a union in which someone can thaw out after earlier, unhappy relationships. A room with a lit stove after last night's blizzard is exactly that.

But the entry point sits on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that the same wish can become resistance. In the poem it is one line: “It is pleasant to think by the stove-bench.” To think, not to go. The trip to the sea is discussed for the fourth summer running. A job offer in another city is turned down because “we're so happy here”. The flat has to be perfect before life in it can start. Comfort works like a stove: it warms as long as someone feeds it, and it keeps hold of whoever sits by it.

The Empress's downside shows up in scenes. The warm home turns out not to be quite their own: the parents' flat, the mother's dacha, her opinion on the renovation — and the couple has to step out from under the family's influence. Money comes in waves, feast or famine. One grows, the other stays by the stove-bench, and for that partner the room slowly turns into a waiting room. Sometimes one of the two is looked after like a child, and the warmth becomes a nursery.

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings for The Empress, right after fruitfulness come “action, initiative”. For this card a home is a beginning, not the last stop. The couple enters its task through the room, but the task lies beyond the door.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: “but now… look out of the window” (19 — The Sun)
paragraphs: The middle shows how the couple travels from the shared home to its main task. For 3-19-7 it travels in the light. Such couples are visible from afar: warm, busy, hospitable, each good at their own work, and one's success spurs the other on. Friends call them the brightest couple they know. Benebell Wen is direct about The Sun in readings about love and relationships: “It could suggest a power couple.”

The shadow of this light is hidden in the second stanza: “And you sat there sad — / But now… look out of the window.” Nobody asks why the beloved was sad. Last night is not talked about — it is flooded with sunlight. Lisovskaya's list of The Sun's tasks has exactly this: not knowing how to talk about problems, and holding feelings back. In real life it sounds like “Oh, come on, look what a day it is!” The one already at the window sincerely wants to share the light. The one still under last night's moon hears: sadness is not done here.

Hence The Sun's other downsides. “It's time, my beauty, wake up” is the timetable of whoever woke first: the day is wondrous, so everyone must get up. Inflated expectations: the sun is out, so we must be happy. Comparisons: “everyone else has proper weekends, and we…”. One partner's win becomes shared when that is convenient, and personal when recognition is wanted. Or the reverse: one disappears into work, the other entirely into the partner.

**A couple's strong Sun is a light in which both can be seen: the one at the window and the one still by the stove-bench.** Such light does not cancel last night's blizzard; it lets someone talk about it.

sections.h2: Main task: “the shore that is dear to me” (7 — The Chariot)
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is read first of all through its downside: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. For 3-19-7 this is The Chariot — direction, will, the skill of steering. Wen writes that “the card affirms movement in the right direction”, and in reverse her first advice is that “the Seeker must reconsider direction”.

The first scene is one person's shore dressed up as a shared one. One partner says “we”: we're moving to the sea, we're starting a business, we're going to Lake Baikal. The other “gives in to the run”. For months all is well, the sleigh flies, and then it turns out the shore was “dear to me” from the very start. Among Lisovskaya's tasks for The Chariot is the demand that a partner give up their own goals for someone else's.

The second scene is two drivers in one sleigh. Each pulls the reins towards their own city, holiday, whose career matters more right now. Lisovskaya calls this a rivalry for leadership, and separately names the balance between career and relationship.

The third scene: the horse is driving. The mortgage, the children's timetable, projects that pull forward on their own. Nobody asked where they are going: “let us give ourselves up to the run of the impatient horse”. The Chariot also has a passive downside — aimlessness: “let us visit the empty fields”, take a drive and see what happens. The passion of the early years fades, and the sleigh goes round in circles.

Lisovskaya's recommendations for The Chariot read as if copied from this poem. Don't rush the partner — yet the horse is “impatient”, and the beauty is woken at dawn. Define the roles clearly, with nothing left unsaid — yet nobody in the poem takes the reins. Let each have their own achievement — yet only one shore is named. When it works, such a couple is like a team: they decide together and fast, each has their own path but they walk side by side, and a move to a place chosen by both fills them up. The Chariot at its best is often looking for “a home of its own” — that is, it comes back to The Empress, where the tail began.

Three years before “Winter Morning”, in November–December 1826, Pushkin wrote the same thing in reverse. “Through the wavy mists / The moon makes its way”, “along the dull winter road / A swift troika runs”, a lone traveller, a coachman driving. “Dull, sad… tomorrow, Nina, / Tomorrow, back with my dear, / I'll lose myself by the fireplace, / Gaze and never gaze my fill.” And at the end: “Dozing, my coachman has fallen silent.”

The draft of that poem has lines that never made the final text: “I'll be by the fireplace tomorrow / In your bright room.” At night the bright room is a lone traveller's dream. Three years later it stands in verse for real: “The whole room is lit / With an amber gleam.” In the same 1826 draft a line is crossed out: “The fir silvers under the hoarfrost.” In the morning poem the fir is back — and now, in the sun, it is green: “And the fir is green through the hoarfrost.” One fir: silver at night, green in the morning.

Two poems, two states of a 3-19-7 couple. At night on the road they long for the fireplace; in the morning by the stove the road pulls at them. At night a stranger drives, and he has dozed off; in the morning the beloved dozes, and the horse drives. The Chariot's task is to stop swinging between these two longings: to hold the reins themselves and go where both have named. For couples where the second partner has the tail 21-10-7, “Winter Road” sounds especially close: one of the two already has a troika of their own, and the other has the moon.

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen saw in these cards
paragraphs: Waite reports the reading of Court de Gébelin, the eighteenth-century writer who first declared the tarot an ancient Egyptian book: “M. Court de Gebelin said that it was Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter.” Waite himself disagrees: “We know now that Osiris rising from the dead is not represented by such obvious symbolism.” Yet for the 3-19-7 tail the old reading works as a key. There is no gap here between The Sun and The Chariot: The Chariot is the sun set in motion. “Frost and sun — a wondrous day!” — and a sleigh.

Another detail in Waite is who pulled the chariot. He takes the sphinxes from Éliphas Lévi; “in the eighteenth century white horses were yoked to the car”, and “other animals than horses have also been used to draw the currus triumphalis, as, for example, a lion and a leopard.” In Pushkin's sleigh there is a “little brown mare”. A humbler team for this card is hard to imagine. This couple's triumph is a domestic one: not an entry into a conquered city but a drive to the shore and back, to the stove.

The most surprising thing Waite writes is about The Sun. Older cards, he says, showed “a wall suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden—wherein are two children”, “gambolling, or running hand in hand”. According to Lévi, these are “sometimes replaced by a spinner unwinding destinies, and otherwise by a much better symbol—a naked child mounted on a white horse and displaying a scarlet standard.” **A walled garden, a spinner and a rider: read this card's history through the tail, and the whole tail fits inside it.** The wall is The Empress's home, the spinner of destinies is kin to The Wheel of Fortune hidden in the number 19, and the rider is the horse that leads to The Chariot.

In the centre of 82.2% of these couples stands Temperance. Waite writes that “when the rule of it obtains in our consciousness, it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures. Under that rule we know in our rational part something of whence we came and whither we are going.” For this couple the answer to The Chariot's main question lies not on the road but in their shared atmosphere.

Wen adds two important things to The Chariot. Here there will be “travel not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition”: the chariot goes out for bounty. For this couple the natural place to bring that bounty is the home where the tail began — that part is our reading. The badge on the chariot, Wen says, carries the traditional meaning of “the union of the external sphere of rulership by man and the internal sphere of rulership by woman”; for a couple what matters is not who is which but the link itself — the road and the home. Even Wen's elements follow the course of the morning: The Empress is Earth, The Sun is Fire, The Chariot is Water. The earth of the home, the fire of the stove and the sun, and the stream that “glitters under the ice” — water that has not stopped beneath the winter crust.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: frost and sun in one cup
paragraphs: “Frost and sun” are two opposite states in a single line. That is the language of Temperance, which stands in the centre for 82.2% of couples with the 3-19-7 tail. In Lisovskaya's account, Temperance in a couple's atmosphere means disputes settled by talking, a balance of activity and rest, peace of mind valued above things. On the downside, one always gives way while the other does not even notice. For a couple with an impatient horse, Temperance's main recommendation sounds almost like an answer: learn to wait for the right moment and look for the middle instead of the extremes. Temperance in the centre is the brake The Chariot lacks.

In 17.8% of couples The Hierophant stands in the centre. Then the atmosphere rests on shared views and on authority accepted freely. The downside is lecturing: “that's all wrong”, “I know better where we're going”. Here the sleigh's route risks becoming a lesson.

The couple's values — what the union exists for — come in two kinds, and the difference shows in one of Pushkin's verbs: “let us give ourselves up”. In 67.3% of such couples the values are The Lovers: giving themselves up as a shared choice, a decision made by both even in small things. In 32.7% they are The Devil: giving themselves up as being carried away, a passion that sweeps them along. In Lisovskaya's account The Devil at its best is strong attachment and readiness to change for love, and at its worst the wish to possess the partner. In the example couple the values are The Devil.

sections.h2: The strong version: a sleigh with two drivers
paragraphs: The 3-19-7 tail is neither a verdict nor a prediction. It shows where the couple stumbles, and almost every scene of “Winter Morning” hints at what can be done differently.

ul: Before calling the other to the window, ask about last night: why the beloved “sat there sad”. The couple's Sun does not have to cancel the moon.
Let the one who is dozing wake up on their own. The timetable of whoever got up first is not a shared one.
Name the shore together — or take turns: one partner's this time, the other's next. Check the word “we” in plans: whose shore is it really?
Decide the route before harnessing, not on the move. People hold the reins, not the horse.
Don't put out the stove when leaving. Home is the base to return to with the bounty: a decision, a new place, a shared project.
Leave each partner their own road beside the shared one. When The Chariot works, each goes their own way, but side by side.

paragraphs: The last stanza of “Winter Morning” can sound different for such a couple. “But you know — shouldn't we have the little brown mare harnessed to the sleigh?” — and the reply is not a silent “let us give ourselves up” but a question in return: “Where shall we go?” **Once the shore is named by both, the impatient horse stops being the driver and becomes just a horse.**

ul: A. S. Pushkin. “Zimneye utro” (Winter Morning; 3 November 1829, Pavlovskoye; the almanac Tsarskoye Selo for 1830). “Zimnyaya doroga” (Winter Road, 1826) and the variants of its draft autograph — from the academic edition.
A. E. Waite. The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, 1922 reissue): The Empress, The Chariot, Temperance, The Sun — symbolism and historical descriptions of the cards.
Benebell Wen. Holistic Tarot (2015): Key 3, Key 7, Key 19.
Yuliana Lisovskaya. Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and the energies 3, 5, 6, 7, 14, 15, 19.
Calculations and statistics — the site's engine, run over all dates.

**M · Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** Where the couple starts: a shared home, warmth, growth, the words “our place”. The point sits on the line of tasks, and the same comfort can turn into resistance: nobody wants to leave a warm room.

**N · Middle of the task — 19, The Sun.** How the couple travels: brightly, openly, in plain view. The same brightness teaches them to skip over yesterday's sadness: “but now… look out of the window”.
**D · Main task — 7, The Chariot.** Direction and reins: where the sleigh is going, whose shore it is and who is driving — the two of them or an impatient horse.

intro: Pushkin fitted this whole plot into the thirty lines of “Winter Morning”. Every Russian child learns the poem at school, and almost nobody notices that it is a morning for two: with last night left unspoken and with a question that stays open in the final line.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3-19-7 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that enters it through a shared wish for home and warmth (The Empress, 3), lives it out brightly and in plain view (The Sun, 19), and learns the main thing — direction: deciding together where to go, and handing the reins neither to one partner nor to inertia (The Chariot, 7).

The middle of a couple's tail is built from the middles of the partners' personal tails, not from its ends. In these couples it is always 10 + 9: one partner's Wheel of Fortune and the other's Hermit. Reducing the ends would give 10, and The Wheel really is hidden inside The Sun — as a term of the sum, not as the result.

faq.q: Can 3-19-7 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With a task of 7, an entry of 3 is impossible for any centre, and the middle of a personal tail would be 3 + 7 = 10. The 3-19-7 tail only appears between two people.

faq.q: How rare is the couple tail 3-19-7?
faq.a: It occurs in roughly one couple in 1,366 (0.073%) and ranks 85th among the 97 couple tails. It forms from two combinations of personal tails: 21-10-16 + 9-9-18 (82%) or 21-10-7 + 9-9-18 (18%).

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The Empress, The Sun and The Chariot appear in a couple's tail only in the order 3-19-7: entry through the home, the middle in the light, the task on the road.

faq.q: Is this an unfavourable tail for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes not the fate of the union but its main lesson. The cards do not predict events or grade the relationship: they show where the couple finds things easy (home and light) and what it is worth learning together (a shared direction).

report: In Pushkin's “Winter Morning” the word “I” appears exactly once — as the last word of the poem. Before it there is only “you”: you are dozing, you remember, you sat there sad. These thirty lines, learnt by every Russian schoolchild, turn out to be a precise portrait of a couple with the karmic tail 3-19-7.

unit.title: Sleigh for two, shore for one

captions.M: To want a warm home and a shared “our place”
captions.N: To live brightly in view, not drowning sadness in sunlight
captions.D: To name the shore together and hold the reins yourselves

unit.meaning: Your task is to choose the route together: name a shared shore, take the reins and not hand them to an impatient horse.
